title: Design a Rate Limiter
oneLiner: A distributed API rate limiter as a 45-minute design round: algorithms, atomic counters in Redis, and what happens when the limiter fails.
keyTakeaway: A rate limiter sits on every request, so it has to be cheap, shared and harmless when broken. Keep counters in a sharded Redis close to the gateways and update them with one atomic Lua script, pick the algorithm per limit (token bucket for API keys, sliding window counter for long windows), and fail open to a local fallback rather than turning a cache outage into an API outage.
explanation:
Same format as the other walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare it with the model answer and tick what you covered. If you haven't done the Rate Limiting building-block lesson, do it first: it compares the algorithms on the same traffic, and this round assumes you know how each one works.

What makes this problem different is that the limiter is not the product; it's a component on the hot path of every other product. That puts the difficulty in three places. First, the budget: the check gets about a millisecond, so it can afford one round trip to an in-memory store and nothing more, and the estimation stage should show that counter operations (several per request), not API requests, size that store. Second, correctness under concurrency: a hundred gateways updating the same counter will break a read-then-write implementation, and even INCR followed by EXPIRE has a gap that can block a client forever. Third, failure: the interviewer will ask what happens when Redis is down, and "the API goes down too" is the wrong answer.

Expect the deep dive to start with algorithms and move quickly to the distributed parts: atomicity, local versus global counting (accuracy against latency), multi-region limits, and fail open versus fail closed. Name the trade-off each time, for example how much overshoot local token leases allow and why that's acceptable for a 10,000-per-second limit but not for 5 login attempts a minute. Good follow-ups to prepare for: "one customer sends half our traffic: what breaks?" and "someone pushed a rule that limits everyone to one request a minute: how would you have caught it?"
